subject_line: Your labs changed. Your effort didn't. What gives?
opening: Hey, it's Chloe. This week we've got a story that's going to hit close to home for anyone who's done everything right and still got a number back that made them panic. Plus Marcus has a lunch fix for those of you eating sad cold meat at your desk, and Sarah's digging into something most people on carnivore completely overlook until it bites them. Let's get into it.

hero.title: Suddenly Sick After Eating Meat Months In
hero.teaser: Six solid months on carnivore. You've figured out your cuts, your timing, your portions. And then one day, the meat that used to feel amazing starts turning your stomach. It's confusing, and honestly a little scary. Sarah breaks down four common reasons this happens months in, and one of them isn't something you can tweak your way out of. You'll want to know which one before you just push through.

supporting.title: The Fat to Protein Ratio That Stalls Fat Loss
supporting.teaser: Marcus found the number that quietly drifts on most people, and it's not the one they're tracking.

supporting.title: Potassium on Carnivore: Why Pills Won't Cut It
supporting.teaser: Sarah explains the legal reason your potassium tablet is basically useless, and where the real amount has to come from.

supporting.title: What to Say When They Ask About Your Plate
supporting.teaser: Chloe's got a better script than 'well actually, insulin...' for the next time someone corners you at a party.

community_pulse.question: I lost a lot of weight on carnivore, my blood sugar was doing great, and now a year and a half in my fasting glucose is creeping back up. I didn't change anything. What's happening?
community_pulse.answer: This one genuinely needs a conversation with your doctor, not a forum. That said, many long-term carnivore members find that a rise in fasting glucose after significant weight loss can reflect a few different things, including a normal physiological adaptation some call 'glucose sparing,' where your body preserves glucose for the tissues that need it. It's also worth knowing that stopping a medication like metformin changes the picture significantly. Bring the full timeline to your doctor, including when you stopped the medication, and ask them to look at fasting insulin alongside glucose.

community_pulse.question: I'm worried that eating high-calorie foods like bacon, eggs, and ribeye will make it impossible to lose weight. How does anyone actually succeed on this eating enough fat?
community_pulse.answer: It's one of the most common sticking points people bring up, and it makes total sense if you've been counting calories for years. Many people find that the hunger-regulating effect of protein and fat means they naturally eat less overall, without tracking every bite. The comparison to low-fat diets breaks down pretty fast once you're a few weeks in and realizing you're actually satisfied between meals.

community_pulse.question: My skin has been a disaster for years. Could changing what I eat actually make a difference?
community_pulse.answer: Community members report this more than almost anything else, and it's one of the most motivating things to see. The timeline varies a lot, but many people share that skin changes, including acne clearing up, tend to show up somewhere in the first three to six months. Nobody can promise a specific outcome, but it's worth knowing you're not the only one who's experienced this, not by a long shot.

try_this_week: Track your protein grams for just three days, not calories, just protein. Marcus makes the case that most stalls come down to a fat-to-protein ratio that quietly drifted in the wrong direction. Pull out whatever you're eating on a typical day, look up the protein number, and see if it's actually where you think it is. Three days of data tells you more than a month of guessing.
looking_ahead: Next week we're getting into something most carnivore resources skip entirely, and it explains why some people feel electric on this diet while others just feel okay. You won't want to miss it.
